question: A tenant signs a one-year lease at $1,050 per month rent. Under 68 P.S. Section 250.511a, what is the MAXIMUM security deposit the landlord may collect at signing?
choice_a: $2,100 (two months' rent)
choice_b: $1,050 (one month's rent)
choice_c: $3,150 (three months' rent)
choice_d: There is no dollar cap as long as it is disclosed in the lease
explanation: Section 250.511a caps the first-year security deposit at two months' rent. At $1,050/month, two months' rent is $2,100 -- the maximum the landlord may lawfully collect at lease signing.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511a (confirmed via research pass on PA security deposit caps)

question: A landlord collected $2,000 (two months' rent at $1,000/month) as a security deposit in year one of a tenancy. The tenant renews for a second year with the same landlord. What must the landlord do with the deposit under 250.511a?
choice_a: Refund $1,000 to the tenant, since the cap drops to one month's rent ($1,000) beginning in year two
choice_b: Retain the full $2,000 for as long as the tenancy continues
choice_c: Collect an additional $1,000 to bring the deposit to three months' rent
choice_d: Transfer the entire $2,000 to the Real Estate Recovery Fund
explanation: Once a tenancy enters its second year, the maximum permissible deposit drops to one month's rent. Here, that is $1,000, so the landlord must refund the $1,000 held in excess of the new cap.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511a (confirmed via research pass)

question: A landlord already holds two months' rent collected at the start of a tenancy in year one. At the year-three lease renewal, may the landlord collect an ADDITIONAL deposit to bring the total held to three months' rent?
choice_a: No -- 250.511a never permits collecting more than two months' rent in total, and by year two the permissible cap has already dropped to one month's rent
choice_b: Yes, as long as the increase is stated in the renewal lease
choice_c: Yes, but only with the tenant's written consent
choice_d: Yes, if the rent itself increased at renewal
explanation: Section 250.511a's caps run only downward over time -- two months' rent in year one, one month's rent from year two onward -- with no mechanism allowing a landlord to increase a deposit above the original first-year maximum at a later renewal.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511a (confirmed via research pass)

question: When a security deposit exceeding $100 held more than two years must be placed in an interest-bearing escrow account under 68 P.S. Section 250.511b, what administrative fee is the landlord entitled to retain?
choice_a: A sum equivalent to 1% per annum of the security money deposited, in lieu of all other administrative and custodial expenses
choice_b: A flat $100 processing fee regardless of the deposit amount
choice_c: 10% of the interest earned, with no cap on additional administrative charges
choice_d: No administrative fee is permitted -- all interest earned belongs to the tenant
explanation: Section 250.511b entitles the landlord to retain, as administrative expenses, a sum equal to 1% per annum on the security money deposited in the interest-bearing escrow account -- this 1% is expressly 'in lieu of all other administrative and custodial expenses.'
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511b (confirmed via research pass citing statutory text)

question: Under 250.511b, what type of financial institution must hold a Pennsylvania landlord's interest-bearing security deposit escrow account?
choice_a: One regulated by the Federal Reserve Board or the Pennsylvania Department of Banking
choice_b: Any institution the landlord personally selects, with no regulatory requirement
choice_c: Only a federally chartered credit union
choice_d: Only the same bank that holds the broker's general business account
explanation: Section 250.511b requires the escrow deposit to be held at a financial institution regulated by either the Federal Reserve Board or the Pennsylvania Department of Banking -- ensuring the funds sit in a properly regulated depository.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511b (confirmed via research pass)

question: Under 250.511b, when does a landlord's obligation to begin paying accrued escrow interest to the tenant first arise?
choice_a: Only after the second anniversary of the deposit of the escrow funds, with payment then made annually on the lease's commencement anniversary
choice_b: Immediately upon depositing the funds into the escrow account
choice_c: Only when the tenant formally requests an accounting
choice_d: Only at the termination of the tenancy, regardless of how long the deposit was held
explanation: The interest-payment obligation under Section 250.511b applies only after the second anniversary of the deposit of escrow funds; from that point, interest is paid to the tenant annually on the anniversary of the lease's commencement.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511b (confirmed via research pass)

question: A tenant's security deposit is $80, held by the landlord for five years. Is the landlord required to place this deposit in an interest-bearing escrow account under 250.511b?
choice_a: No -- the $100 threshold is not met, so the interest-escrow requirement does not apply regardless of how long the deposit is held
choice_b: Yes, because the deposit has been held more than two years
choice_c: Yes, all security deposits regardless of amount must earn interest after two years
choice_d: It depends on whether the tenant requests it in writing
explanation: Section 250.511b's interest-escrow requirement is triggered only when a deposit BOTH exceeds $100 AND is held more than two years. Here, the $80 deposit never crosses the $100 threshold, so the escrow/interest requirement never applies no matter how long it is held.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.511b (confirmed via research pass)

question: If a Pennsylvania landlord fails to provide the tenant a written itemized list of damage deductions within 30 days of lease termination, what happens to the landlord's right to withhold ANY portion of the deposit, regardless of actual damages?
choice_a: The landlord forfeits all right to withhold any portion of the deposit for damages
choice_b: The landlord may still withhold amounts for damages, just with a delayed accounting
choice_c: The landlord's right to withhold is unaffected as long as the deposit is eventually itemized
choice_d: The landlord may withhold up to 50% of the deposit without providing any list
explanation: Under 68 P.S. Section 250.512, missing the 30-day deadline to provide the itemized list causes the landlord to forfeit ALL right to withhold any portion of the security deposit for damages -- a separate, automatic consequence from the double-damages remedy that applies specifically to willful noncompliance.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.512 (confirmed via research pass)

question: Does the 30-day deadline in 250.512 govern only the landlord's DUTY TO PROVIDE the itemized list, or does it also govern the duty to actually PAY the tenant the refund difference?
choice_a: It governs both -- the landlord must both provide the itemized list AND pay the tenant the difference between the deposit and actual damages within the same 30-day window
choice_b: It governs only the itemized list; payment of any refund may be made at the landlord's convenience
choice_c: It governs only the payment obligation; there is no deadline for providing the list itself
choice_d: Neither obligation has a statutory deadline under 250.512
explanation: Section 250.512 imposes the 30-day deadline on both duties -- providing the written itemized list of damages AND paying the tenant any refund difference. Failure to meet either deadline exposes the landlord to liability.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.512 (confirmed via research pass)

question: A landlord provides the tenant a timely itemized damage list on day 25 after lease termination, showing $200 owed back to the tenant, but does not actually pay that $200 until day 45. Has the landlord complied with 250.512?
choice_a: No -- because the payment itself was late, the landlord remains liable in assumpsit for double the amount wrongfully withheld, even though the list was timely
choice_b: Yes -- once the itemized list is timely provided, the payment deadline no longer applies
choice_c: Yes -- the landlord has 60 days to pay after providing the list
choice_d: No, but the only consequence is a formal warning from the Real Estate Commission
explanation: Timely provision of the itemized list does not excuse a late refund payment -- both the list and the payment of any difference must occur within 30 days of termination. A late payment still exposes the landlord to double-damages liability under Section 250.512.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.512 (confirmed via research pass)

question: Under 250.512, in what type of civil action would a tenant sue a landlord to recover double the wrongfully withheld security deposit?
choice_a: An action in assumpsit
choice_b: An action in ejectment
choice_c: A quiet title action
choice_d: An action before the State Real Estate Commission only
explanation: Section 250.512 specifically provides that a landlord who fails to comply with the 30-day itemization/payment requirement 'shall be liable in assumpsit' to the tenant for double the wrongfully withheld amount -- assumpsit being the traditional contract-based civil action.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.512 (confirmed via research pass)

question: Under 68 P.S. Section 250.501, must a landlord's notice to quit be given to the tenant in writing?
choice_a: Yes -- Section 250.501 requires the landlord to notify the tenant to remove from the premises in writing
choice_b: No -- a verbal notice satisfies the statute as long as a witness is present
choice_c: No -- written notice is only required for commercial tenancies
choice_d: Written notice is only required if the tenant demands it
explanation: Section 250.501 requires the landlord to notify the tenant 'in writing' to remove from the premises -- a foundational, statute-level formality underlying all of the section's notice-period tiers.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.501 (confirmed via research pass)

question: For a MOBILE HOME PARK tenancy with a lease term of less than one year or an indeterminate term (e.g., month-to-month), how many days' notice to quit does 250.501 require for termination of the term or forfeiture for breach -- compared to the 15-day notice for an equivalent standard residential tenancy?
choice_a: 30 days for the mobile home park tenancy, versus 15 days for a standard residential tenancy of the same length
choice_b: The same 15 days that applies to standard residential tenancies
choice_c: 10 days, shorter than the standard residential notice
choice_d: There is no separate mobile home provision -- all tenancies use the same notice tiers
explanation: Section 250.501 sets a longer 30-day notice period for mobile home park tenancies of less than one year or an indeterminate term, in contrast to the shorter 15-day period that applies to an equivalent standard (non-mobile-home) residential tenancy.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.501 (confirmed via research pass on the mobile home park notice provisions)

question: For a MOBILE HOME PARK tenancy with a lease term of one year or more, how many days' (or months') notice to quit does 250.501 require for termination of the term or forfeiture for breach?
choice_a: Three months, compared to just 30 days for a standard residential tenancy of the same length
choice_b: 30 days, the same as a standard residential tenancy of the same length
choice_c: 15 days
choice_d: One year
explanation: Section 250.501 requires three months' notice to quit for mobile home park tenancies with a lease term of one year or more -- substantially longer than the 30-day notice period that applies to a standard residential lease of the same length.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.501 (confirmed via research pass)

question: For NONPAYMENT OF RENT in a MOBILE HOME PARK tenancy, 250.501 sets a seasonal notice period rather than the flat 10-day notice used for standard residential tenancies. If notice is given between April 1 and September 1, how many days' notice must the mobile home tenant receive?
choice_a: 15 days
choice_b: 10 days, the same as a standard residential tenancy
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: 45 days
explanation: For mobile home park nonpayment-of-rent notices given between April 1 and September 1, Section 250.501 requires 15 days' notice -- longer than the 10-day period for standard residential nonpayment, and shorter than the 30-day period that applies to mobile home nonpayment notices given the rest of the year.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.501 (confirmed via research pass on mobile home seasonal nonpayment notice)

question: For NONPAYMENT OF RENT in a MOBILE HOME PARK tenancy, if notice is given between September 1 and April 1 (the colder months), how many days' notice must 250.501 give the tenant?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 15 days, the same as the April-to-September period
choice_c: 10 days
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: Section 250.501 extends the mobile home nonpayment notice period to 30 days when notice is given between September 1 and April 1, providing longer notice during the colder months than the 15-day period that applies from April 1 to September 1.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.501 (confirmed via research pass)

question: Among the notice-to-quit periods set by 250.501, which scenario requires the LONGEST notice to the tenant?
choice_a: A mobile home park tenancy with a lease term of one year or more, terminated at the end of the term (three months' notice)
choice_b: A standard residential tenancy with a term of more than one year (30 days' notice)
choice_c: A standard residential tenancy for nonpayment of rent (10 days' notice)
choice_d: A standard residential tenancy of one year or less (15 days' notice)
explanation: Of all the notice tiers in Section 250.501, the three-month notice required for a mobile home park tenancy of one year or more is the longest -- longer than any standard residential notice period, which tops out at 30 days.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.501 (confirmed via research pass, comparison of notice tiers)

question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.321, when does a broker's duty to pay over a tenant's security deposit -- held by the broker on behalf of a lessor-client -- actually arise?
choice_a: When the tenancy ends
choice_b: The moment the deposit is first collected from the tenant
choice_c: Only when the lessor-client demands the funds in writing
choice_d: It never arises -- the broker may retain the deposit as part of the rental management account indefinitely
explanation: Section 35.321 specifies that if a broker holds a security deposit belonging to another under a lease, the broker's duty to pay over that deposit arises when the tenancy ends -- not before.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.321 (confirmed via research pass)

question: Apart from the rental management exception, what is a Pennsylvania broker's GENERAL duty under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.321 regarding money the broker receives that belongs to another party to a transaction?
choice_a: Deposit it into an escrow account at a Federally or State-insured bank or depository, held pending consummation of the transaction or its prior termination without dispute
choice_b: Deposit it into the broker's personal checking account for convenience
choice_c: Forward it directly to the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission for safekeeping
choice_d: Hold it in cash on the broker's premises until the transaction closes
explanation: Section 35.321's general rule requires a broker to deposit money received on behalf of another into an escrow account at a Federally or State-insured bank or depository, pending consummation of the transaction or a prior, non-disputed termination -- the rental-management account is a specific, narrower exception to this general escrow duty.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.321 (confirmed via research pass)

question: A licensed salesperson, acting under a broker's supervision, shows a vacant rental unit to a prospective tenant and collects a completed rental application to pass along to the broker. Is this permitted under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.287?
choice_a: Yes -- this assistance does not involve independently negotiating lease terms or executing the lease, so it falls within the salesperson's permitted supervised role
choice_b: No -- salespersons may never have any contact with prospective tenants
choice_c: No -- only associate brokers may show rental units
choice_d: Yes, but only if the salesperson has at least five years of licensure
explanation: Section 35.287 permits a salesperson to assist with property management under the broker's supervision and control. Showing a unit and collecting an application does not cross into independently negotiating lease terms or executing the lease, so it remains within the permitted scope.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.287 (confirmed via research pass)

question: A licensed salesperson, without consulting the supervising broker, agrees to a reduced monthly rent with a prospective tenant and signs the lease on the lessor's behalf. Does this comply with 49 Pa. Code Section 35.287?
choice_a: No -- 35.287 specifically bars a salesperson from independently negotiating lease terms or executing a lease on the lessor's behalf, regardless of the broker's general supervision
choice_b: Yes -- once a salesperson is assigned a property management file, full negotiating and signing authority transfers to the salesperson
choice_c: Yes, as long as the lessor is notified after the fact
choice_d: It complies as long as the reduced rent is still within the listed price range
explanation: Section 35.287 draws a bright line: a salesperson may assist with property management under supervision, but may not independently negotiate lease terms or execute a lease on the lessor's behalf. Doing so here -- unilaterally lowering rent and signing the lease -- exceeds the salesperson's permitted authority.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.287 (confirmed via research pass)

question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.287, who bears ultimate responsibility for property management functions performed by a supervised salesperson?
choice_a: The supervising broker
choice_b: The salesperson alone, once assigned to the file
choice_c: The lessor-client directly
choice_d: The Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission, as the licensing authority
explanation: Because Section 35.287 requires a salesperson's property management assistance to be supervised and controlled by the employing broker, ultimate responsibility for those functions rests with the broker, not the salesperson performing the day-to-day tasks.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.287 (confirmed via research pass)

question: What legal doctrine did the Pennsylvania Supreme Court establish in Pugh v. Holmes (486 Pa. 272, 1979) regarding residential leases?
choice_a: An implied warranty of habitability, abolishing the older doctrine of caveat emptor and tying the tenant's obligation to pay rent to the landlord's duty to maintain habitable premises
choice_b: That security deposits are unconstitutional under the Pennsylvania Constitution
choice_c: That all residential leases in Pennsylvania must be in writing to be enforceable
choice_d: That landlords have no maintenance obligations whatsoever under Pennsylvania common law
explanation: In Pugh v. Holmes, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court abolished the doctrine of caveat emptor as applied to residential leases and recognized an implied warranty of habitability, making the tenant's rent obligation dependent on the landlord maintaining the premises in habitable condition.
source_note: Pugh v. Holmes, 486 Pa. 272 (1979) (confirmed via research pass citing Pennsylvania Supreme Court case law)

question: Under the implied warranty of habitability recognized in Pugh v. Holmes, what remedies does a Pennsylvania tenant have when a landlord fails to maintain the premises in habitable condition?
choice_a: Remedies including rent abatement and repair-and-deduct, among other available remedies for the landlord's breach
choice_b: No remedy -- the warranty is aspirational and creates no enforceable tenant right
choice_c: The tenant's only remedy is immediate lease termination, with no right to remain and seek abatement
choice_d: The tenant must vacate within 10 days or waive the claim entirely
explanation: The implied warranty of habitability recognized in Pugh v. Holmes gives tenants remedies such as rent abatement and repair-and-deduct when a landlord fails to maintain habitable conditions -- part of the broader shift away from caveat emptor in Pennsylvania residential leases.
source_note: Pugh v. Holmes, 486 Pa. 272 (1979) (confirmed via research pass); hedge: remedy list summarized from secondary legal-commentary sources, not a direct statutory citation

question: Does the implied warranty of habitability recognized in Pugh v. Holmes apply to COMMERCIAL leases in Pennsylvania the same way it applies to residential leases?
choice_a: No -- Pugh v. Holmes addressed residential leases specifically, and the implied warranty of habitability is a residential-tenancy doctrine
choice_b: Yes -- the warranty applies identically to all leases, commercial and residential alike
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial leases of retail space
choice_d: The warranty applies to commercial leases but not residential leases
explanation: Pugh v. Holmes and the implied warranty of habitability it established apply specifically to residential leases; Pennsylvania commercial leases remain governed by traditional contract principles rather than this residential-tenant protection.
source_note: Pugh v. Holmes, 486 Pa. 272 (1979) (confirmed via research pass)

question: Prior to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's 1979 decision in Pugh v. Holmes, what legal doctrine governed a residential tenant's obligation to pay rent regardless of the property's condition?
choice_a: Caveat emptor ("let the buyer beware")
choice_b: The implied warranty of habitability
choice_c: Strict landlord liability for all property defects
choice_d: The doctrine of constructive eviction only
explanation: Before Pugh v. Holmes, Pennsylvania residential leases were governed by caveat emptor -- tenants were obligated to pay rent regardless of the property's condition, with no implied duty on the landlord to maintain habitability. Pugh v. Holmes abolished this doctrine for residential leases.
source_note: Pugh v. Holmes, 486 Pa. 272 (1979) (confirmed via research pass)

question: May a Pennsylvania landlord lawfully regain possession of a rental unit by changing the locks, removing the tenant's belongings, or shutting off utilities, without first obtaining a court order?
choice_a: No -- such "self-help" eviction is unlawful in Pennsylvania regardless of the tenant's default; the landlord must use the judicial eviction process
choice_b: Yes, as long as the tenant is more than 30 days behind on rent
choice_c: Yes, but only after giving the statutory notice to quit, with no court filing required
choice_d: Yes, if the lease contains a self-help clause authorizing it
explanation: Pennsylvania law prohibits landlord self-help eviction -- changing locks, removing belongings, or shutting off utilities without a court order is unlawful even where the tenant has defaulted. The landlord must pursue the judicial process under the Landlord and Tenant Act to regain possession.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.513 and related Landlord and Tenant Act possession provisions (confirmed via research pass corroborated across multiple legal-aid and practitioner sources)

question: What is the exclusive lawful method for a Pennsylvania landlord to regain possession of a rental unit from a tenant who refuses to vacate after a valid notice to quit has expired?
choice_a: Filing an action for possession in court and obtaining an Order for Possession, enforced only by a constable or sheriff
choice_b: Personally removing the tenant's belongings from the unit once the notice period expires
choice_c: Shutting off electricity and water service to encourage the tenant to leave voluntarily
choice_d: Filing a complaint with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission, which handles evictions directly
explanation: After a notice to quit expires without the tenant vacating, the landlord's only lawful path to possession is filing an action in court and obtaining an Order for Possession -- which is then enforced exclusively by a constable or sheriff, never by the landlord directly.
source_note: 68 P.S. Section 250.513 and related Landlord and Tenant Act possession provisions (confirmed via research pass)

question: Under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA), may a tenant who enters active military duty (or receives qualifying military orders) terminate a residential lease early without penalty?
choice_a: Yes -- with proper written notice and a copy of the qualifying military orders, the tenant may terminate the lease, with termination taking effect a set period after the next rent due date
choice_b: No -- the SCRA only protects servicemembers from mortgage foreclosure, not residential leases
choice_c: No -- early lease termination for military service is governed solely by state law, and Pennsylvania provides no such protection
choice_d: Yes, but only if the landlord consents in writing
explanation: The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act allows a tenant entering active duty (or receiving qualifying military orders such as a permanent change of station or deployment) to terminate a residential lease early with proper written notice and a copy of the orders, with the termination effective a set period after the next rent due date -- a federal protection layered on top of any state-specific landlord-tenant law.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal servicemember lease-termination protection (50 U.S.C. App. Section 3955 / Servicemembers Civil Relief Act); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory citation

question: Beyond accounting for funds, leasing the property, and collecting rents and security deposits, what other routine responsibility does a property manager typically retain under a standard property management agreement?
choice_a: Arranging routine maintenance and repairs, including turnover/make-ready work on the unit between tenancies
choice_b: Setting the property's assessed value for real estate tax purposes
choice_c: Issuing title insurance policies to prospective tenants
choice_d: Performing the property's structural engineering inspections in place of a licensed engineer
explanation: Alongside accounting, leasing, and rent/deposit collection, a property manager typically also handles routine maintenance and repair coordination -- including preparing a unit for a new tenant between tenancies -- as part of the day-to-day management function tested under the national outline's property management duties.
source_note: hedge: general property management industry practice consistent with the Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, Section V.B.3; not a direct statutory citation

question: In a standard exclusive property management agreement, who generally holds the authority to approve MAJOR CAPITAL expenditures (e.g., a roof replacement) on the managed property, absent express delegation to the manager?
choice_a: The property owner/lessor, not the property manager
choice_b: The property manager, without any owner approval required
choice_c: The tenant currently occupying the unit
choice_d: The Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
explanation: Absent express authority delegated in the management agreement, a property manager's role is generally limited to routine operational decisions -- major capital expenditures remain the owner/lessor's decision, since the manager acts as the owner's agent rather than an independent decision-maker on large capital outlays.
source_note: hedge: general property management agency doctrine; not a direct Pennsylvania statutory citation
